lessons.title: Progressive overload
lessons.summary: Progress means asking your body to handle a little more over time, usually through extra clean reps or a small weight increase.

blocks.text: By the end, you can choose a small next-step progression instead of changing everything at once. [[progressive overload]] means making training gradually harder as a challenge becomes familiar.
More does not mean reckless

Progressive overload is not adding weight at every workout, whatever happens. It means improving the training challenge across many sessions while your reps stay controlled. You might lift more weight, complete more clean reps, add a useful set, or improve your range and control. Think of it like turning a dial, not launching a rocket.

blocks.title: Everyone Is Confused About Progressive Overload
blocks.why: Watch: how progressive overload works (Jeff Nippard).

items.title: Start inside the range
items.text: Imagine your plan says 3 sets of 8–10 reps. You use 20 kg and record 8, 8, and 8 clean reps. This is an example, not a prescription.

items.title: Build reps first
items.text: Across later workouts, keep 20 kg and try to earn more clean reps. Your log might move to 10, 9, and 8, then 10, 10, and 10.

items.title: Add a small amount
items.text: Once every set reaches the top of the range, move to 22.5 kg. Your reps may return near the bottom. That is normal.

items.title: Repeat the climb
items.text: Build the reps again before the next increase. This reps-then-weight loop is called [[double progression]].

blocks.title: Reps or weight can both work
blocks.text: A study in newer lifters found that progressing by repetitions or by load produced similar improvements over its training period. That supports using the option your equipment and program make practical.

params.title: Progress rarely forms a perfect staircase
params.note: Some weeks hold steady or dip. Look for the longer trend.

blocks.caption: Illustration: real progress includes flat days, small dips, and later breakthroughs.

blocks.text: What to do in LiftLog

Follow the Built With Science Upper/Lower routine as written. LiftLog pre-fills your last weight and reps, so the next sensible target is visible. Try to beat one useful detail without changing five others. If technique changes, the comparison is less meaningful. Use [[lesson:tech-choosing-weight|Choosing the right weight]] when a load is clearly too light or too heavy.

left.title: Useful progress
items: One more clean rep at the same weight
The same reps with slightly more weight
Better control at the same weight and reps

right.title: Progress-shaped noise
items: Shortening the movement to claim extra reps
Changing every exercise before trends appear
Adding weight while technique falls apart

takeaways: Progressive overload means gradually increasing a useful training challenge.
Double progression builds reps first, then adds a small amount of weight.
Judge progress across several sessions, not one unusually good or bad day.
LiftLog’s previous-set values make the next sensible target easy to spot.

quiz.q: You reach the top of your rep range on every set with clean form. What is the clearest next step?
options: Add a small amount of weight next time
Change the entire workout next time
Repeat fewer reps with the same weight
quiz.why: In double progression, reaching the top across all sets earns a small load increase. Reps can then return near the range’s bottom.

quiz.q: Your reps rise only because you shorten the movement. Did you clearly progress?
options: Yes, because any extra rep proves progress
No, because the task changed during the comparison
Yes, because range never matters when logging
quiz.why: A shorter movement is a different task. Keep execution comparable so the log reflects a real performance change.

sources.label: American College of Sports Medicine (2009) — Progression models in resistance training
Chaves TS et al. (2024) — Load versus repetition progression protocols

lessons.title: How many sets? Training volume
lessons.summary: Weekly hard sets are a useful way to count training volume, but more work brings diminishing returns and more fatigue.

blocks.text: By the end, you can count useful weekly sets and know when not to add more. [[Training volume]] is the work you perform; for muscle growth, weekly [[hard set|hard sets]] are a practical shortcut.
Count useful sets, not every warm-up

A hard set is challenging enough to be a meaningful growth signal. Easy warm-up sets prepare you, but they are not counted the same way. A pressing set may train several muscles, so set counting is always an estimate. It is a map, not a laboratory scan.

params.label: Weekly hard sets for one muscle

stops.title: Under 5 sets
stops.text: The lowest weekly-dose category in the 2017 review. It can still be useful and leaves room to add work later.

stops.title: 5–9 sets
stops.text: A middle research category. Using it as a beginner starting example is a coaching suggestion, not a proven optimum.

stops.title: 10+ sets
stops.text: A higher-dose category in this review, not a personal target or an unlimited-more-is-better rule.

blocks.caption: These are the 2017 review’s research categories. Choosing the middle band as a beginner starting example is a coaching suggestion, not a proven optimum.

blocks.title: Why we say returns can shrink
blocks.text: The 2017 review found more growth in higher weekly-set categories, but it did not identify one perfect number for every person. Exercise choice, effort, training age and recovery change what you can use.

blocks.title: How Many Sets Per Exercise is BEST?
blocks.why: Watch: choosing a useful number of sets (Renaissance Periodization).

params.title: More volume, smaller extra returns
params.note: The shapes explain diminishing returns. They are not measured values.

blocks.caption: Illustration: useful work can rise while each extra set buys less.

blocks.title: Start with the routine you have
blocks.text: The Built With Science Upper/Lower plan already distributes work across the week. Do not add sets just because a slider has a bigger number. First log the plan consistently and see whether performance rises.
When should volume change?

Keep volume steady while you are progressing and recovering. Consider a small increase only when performance has stalled, technique is sound, effort is appropriate, and recovery is fine. If several exercises slide backward and you feel worn down, more sets are unlikely to be the first answer. Use the checklist in [[lesson:prog-deloads-plateaus|Plateaus and deloads]] before editing the plan.

takeaways: Count challenging working sets, not every warm-up set.
More weekly sets can help, but the extra benefit tends to shrink.
Beginners should start modestly and add work only when results and recovery support it.
A repeatable plan beats chasing the largest possible set count.

quiz.q: Your planned volume is producing steady progress. What should you do first?
options: Double every exercise’s weekly sets
Keep the plan steady and keep logging
Add random sets whenever energy feels high
quiz.why: Volume is already doing its job. More work adds fatigue and is not automatically better.

quiz.q: Which set is least useful to count as a hard growth set?
options: A challenging working set near your limit
A controlled working set that slows near the end
An easy warm-up set used to prepare
quiz.why: Warm-ups are useful preparation, but they do not create the same training challenge as hard working sets.

sources.label: Schoenfeld BJ, Ogborn D, Krieger JW (2017) — Weekly volume dose-response meta-analysis

lessons.title: How often: frequency and splits
lessons.summary: Frequency is how often a muscle trains; a split is how the week is organised. Choose a schedule you can repeat.

blocks.text: By the end, you can choose a weekly split that fits your calendar and spreads work sensibly. [[Training frequency]] is how often a muscle trains; a [[training split]] packages movements across days.
Why train a muscle more than once?

blocks.title: What the updated review found
blocks.text: Training a muscle more often can spread your weekly work across shorter, less tiring sessions. An updated review found no meaningful muscle-growth advantage from higher frequency when weekly volume was equal. Choose a schedule that lets you complete good-quality work and recover.

left.title: Full body
items: Most major muscle groups each session
Works well with fewer training days
Sessions can feel broad and busy

right.title: Upper/lower
items: Upper and lower sessions alternate
Each muscle can appear about twice weekly
Matches LiftLog’s Built With Science routine

left.title: Push-pull-legs
items: Pressing, pulling, and leg days rotate
Can suit people who enjoy more gym days
Missed days may shift the whole rotation

right.title: The best split
items: Fits your real weekly calendar
Lets you recover between similar sessions
Makes the planned weekly work repeatable

blocks.text: The split is packaging

A split is not magic by itself. Muscle growth depends more on useful weekly training than on the name printed above Monday. When weekly volume is similar, several schedules can work. The winning schedule is usually the one you can perform with good effort, sensible recovery, and few skipped sessions.

blocks.title: Which Workout Split Is Actually Best? (Science-Based)
blocks.why: Watch: how common workout splits compare (Jeff Nippard).

blocks.title: Use the plan already loaded
blocks.text: The Built With Science Upper/Lower routine gives each half of your body repeated practice across the week. Keep its order unless your calendar truly demands a change. If you miss a day, resume the sequence instead of cramming everything into one marathon session.

Your week also needs space between hard sessions for the same muscles. Recovery needs vary, so link to [[lesson:rec-rest-days|Rest days and active recovery]] rather than guessing from soreness alone. A schedule that looks elegant on paper but fails every busy week is just decorative stationery.

takeaways: Frequency describes how often a muscle trains; a split organises exercises across the week.
About twice weekly is a practical scheduling option, not a proven requirement for superior growth.
Full body, upper/lower, and push-pull-legs can all work when weekly training is sensible.
Choose the schedule you can repeat, recover from, and fit around real life.

quiz.q: Two plans provide similar weekly work. Which split is the better choice?
options: The one with the most impressive name
The one that fits your week and recovery
The one requiring the longest single session
quiz.why: A split is a way to organise useful work. Consistency and recovery matter more than the label.

quiz.q: You miss an upper-body day in your normal rotation. What is usually sensible?
options: Resume the sequence at the next opportunity
Repeat the last lower session immediately
Combine every missed set into one giant workout
quiz.why: Resuming the sequence protects the plan’s balance without turning one missed day into an excessive catch-up session.

sources.label: Schoenfeld BJ, Grgic J, Krieger J (2019) — Updated resistance-training frequency and hypertrophy meta-analysis

lessons.title: How hard: effort and failure
lessons.summary: Hard sets should approach your clean-rep limit, but reaching failure on every set is unnecessary and can create extra fatigue.

blocks.text: By the end, you can judge whether a set was hard enough without forcing every set to failure. [[RIR]] means “reps in reserve”: clean reps you believe remained.
Use the fuel-gauge idea

Picture a fuel gauge counting down toward empty. Four RIR means you likely had four clean reps left. Zero RIR means no clean rep remained. That endpoint is [[muscular failure]]. Estimating RIR is a skill, so beginners often improve with practice and honest logging.

stops.title: 0 RIR
stops.text: No clean rep remains. This is muscular failure.

stops.title: 1 RIR
stops.text: One clean rep probably remains. The set is very hard.

stops.title: 2 RIR
stops.text: Two clean reps probably remain. This is hard without being all-out.

stops.title: 3 RIR
stops.text: Three clean reps probably remain. This can still be productive.

stops.title: 4 RIR
stops.text: Four clean reps probably remain. Useful for practice or managing fatigue.

blocks.caption: RIR is an estimate of clean reps remaining, not a perfect measurement.

blocks.text: Reviews find that reaching failure is not required for strength or muscle growth. Sets still need enough effort to create a useful challenge. The exact best distance from failure is not settled, and the relationship may not be a simple straight line. “Closer” is not automatically “better” forever.

blocks.title: How To Tell If You're Training Hard Enough (Using Science)
blocks.why: Watch: judging whether a set is hard enough (Jeff Nippard).

left.title: Stopping just short
items: Keeps one or more clean reps available
Usually creates less immediate fatigue
Often suits repeated compound movements

right.title: Reaching failure
items: Confirms no clean rep remains
Can be easier to judge on stable movements
May cost more fatigue for little extra benefit

blocks.title: Technique is the boundary
blocks.text: Stop when another rep would require a major technique change or create pain. Muscular failure is about clean reps, not forcing the weight through any possible path.
What to do on Monday

Follow the routine’s target effort. Record your estimate after the set, before hindsight edits the story. If you finish with four or more clean reps available, the set may be too easy for its goal. If every set becomes an all-out battle, reduce the load or stop sooner. Learn the moment-to-moment skill in [[lesson:tech-choosing-weight|Choosing the right weight]].

takeaways: RIR estimates how many clean reps remained when you stopped.
Training to failure is not required for strength or muscle growth.
Hard, controlled sets can be productive without becoming all-out battles.
Stop when technique breaks down or pain appears.

quiz.q: You finish a set and believe two clean reps remained. What should you log?
options: 0 RIR
2 RIR
4 RIR
quiz.why: RIR records your estimate of clean repetitions still available. Two remaining reps means 2 RIR.

quiz.q: Must every working set reach muscular failure to build muscle?
options: Yes, every set must end at failure
No, challenging non-failure sets can work
Yes, unless the workout feels very long
quiz.why: Meta-analyses do not show that momentary failure is required. Appropriate effort matters, but all-out sets are optional.

sources.label: Grgic J et al. (2022) — Failure versus non-failure training meta-analysis
Refalo MC et al. (2023) — Proximity-to-failure and hypertrophy meta-analysis

lessons.title: Plateaus and deloads
lessons.summary: A plateau is a trend, not one bad workout. Check the basics first; a deload can reduce accumulated fatigue when needed.

blocks.text: By the end, you can tell one rough workout from a real plateau and choose a sensible next step. A [[plateau]] is stalled progress across repeated, comparable sessions.
Troubleshoot before rebuilding everything

groups.title: Check the log
items: Have several comparable sessions actually stalled?
Did range of motion and technique stay consistent?
Did exercise order or equipment change?

groups.title: Check the training
items: Are hard sets challenging enough?
Are you adding extra sets that create fatigue?
Have you followed the program long enough to see a trend?

groups.title: Check recovery
items: Has sleep recently been worse?
Has food intake or body-weight trend changed?
Has work, travel, illness, or life stress risen?

blocks.caption: Tick what you have checked. The list stays on this device until you reset it.

blocks.text: A stalled log can come from many places. The load may be too heavy, effort may be too low, or added volume may exceed your recovery. Sometimes the problem is simply comparison noise: different equipment, shorter movement, or a changed exercise order.
What is a deload?

A [[deload]] is a brief period of reduced training stress. Coaches commonly use it to reduce physical and mental fatigue, improve recovery, and prepare for later training. Research on the best design is limited, so there is no universal deload recipe.

blocks.title: When and How to Deload for SIZE | Hypertrophy Made Simple #10
blocks.why: Watch: when and how a deload can help (Renaissance Periodization).

items.title: Confirm the trend
items.text: Review several comparable sessions. If one workout dipped after a poor day, continue and observe.

items.title: Fix the obvious cause
items.text: Correct inconsistent technique, unrealistic loading, missed sessions, or recovery problems before changing the entire program.

items.title: Reduce training stress
items.text: If fatigue has accumulated, temporarily use fewer hard sets, lighter loads, more reps in reserve, or a combination.

items.title: Return and reassess
items.text: Resume normal training gradually. Use the log to see whether performance and motivation improve.

blocks.title: Deload evidence is still developing
blocks.text: The main deload guidance comes from expert consensus and coaching practice, not a large collection of direct trials. Treat it as a flexible fatigue-management tool, not a mandatory calendar ritual.

LiftLog gives you the evidence needed for this decision: previous weights, reps, and completed sessions. Pair that record with [[lesson:rec-sleep|Sleep]] and [[lesson:rec-stress-overreaching|Stress, fatigue and overreaching]]. If pain, illness, or unusual symptoms drive the decline, do not treat a programming checklist as medical advice.

takeaways: A plateau is repeated stalled performance under comparable conditions, not one bad day.
Check technique, effort, volume, consistency, food, sleep, and life stress before rewriting the plan.
A deload briefly reduces training stress to manage accumulated fatigue.
Deload design is flexible because direct research remains limited.

quiz.q: One workout is worse after a stressful day. Is that clearly a plateau?
options: Yes, one decline proves the program failed
No, look for a repeated comparable trend
Yes, immediately replace every exercise
quiz.why: Single-session performance is noisy. A plateau needs a repeated pattern under reasonably comparable conditions.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a deload?
options: To reduce training stress and manage fatigue
To test your hardest possible lifts
To add extra work before a holiday
quiz.why: A deload lowers training stress for a short period so fatigue can fall before normal training resumes.

sources.label: Bell L et al. (2023) — International Delphi consensus on integrating deloads

lessons.title: Cardio and lifting together
lessons.summary: Cardio supports health and can coexist with lifting. Manage hard sessions so fatigue does not crowd out your priority work.

blocks.text: By the end, you can place cardio beside lifting without treating them as rival sports. Doing both is [[concurrent training]], and the schedule matters more than choosing one camp.
The health target is bigger than the gym

WHO recommends adults complete 150–300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity, or 75–150 minutes of vigorous activity, each week. It also recommends muscle-strengthening work for all major muscle groups on at least 2 days weekly. Your Upper/Lower sessions can cover the strengthening part when performed consistently.

blocks.title: Daily movement counts
blocks.text: Walking, cycling for transport, active chores, and planned cardio all contribute to movement. You do not need to make every health-focused session exhausting.
Will cardio erase your gains?

blocks.title: What the combined-training review found
blocks.text: Combining aerobic and strength training did not meaningfully reduce muscle growth or maximal strength on average. Explosive strength showed a small interference effect, especially when both modes shared one session. For most beginners, this is a scheduling detail, not a reason to avoid cardio.

blocks.title: How To Do Cardio (Without Losing Muscle)
blocks.why: Watch: combining cardio with muscle-focused training (Jeff Nippard).

left.title: When lifting is the priority
items: Lift before hard cardio in the same session
Keep easy cardio genuinely easy
Separate demanding sessions when practical

right.title: When cardio is the priority
items: Do the important cardio while fresh
Place hard leg lifting away from key cardio
Accept that both goals share recovery

items.title: Place your four lifting days
items.text: Keep the Built With Science Upper/Lower sequence as the week’s strength framework.

items.title: Add easy movement
items.text: Use walks or comfortable cardio where they fit. Easy work should not turn every day into a recovery test.

items.title: Place demanding cardio
items.text: Avoid stacking your hardest cardio directly before a lower-body session when leg performance matters.

items.title: Watch the log
items.text: If lower-body performance repeatedly falls, adjust cardio timing, intensity, or total workload instead of abandoning it.

blocks.text: Start below the weekly guideline if you are currently inactive, then build gradually. The target is a weekly total, not a punishment due by Sunday night. If a health condition, pregnancy, pain, or unusual symptoms affect exercise, seek individual guidance rather than using a general lesson as a prescription.

takeaways: Cardio and lifting can coexist without ruining muscle growth or maximal strength.
WHO recommends weekly aerobic activity plus muscle strengthening on at least two days.
Do your priority work while fresh and separate demanding sessions when practical.
Use your lifting log to catch repeated fatigue instead of fearing cardio automatically.

quiz.q: You must lift and do hard cardio in one session, and strength is your priority. What is sensible?
options: Do the lifting first while you are fresh
Do the hardest cardio immediately before lifting
Skip strength work whenever cardio appears
quiz.why: Placing the priority first protects its quality. Hard cardio beforehand can add fatigue to the lifting session.

quiz.q: Does combining cardio and lifting automatically stop muscle growth?
options: Yes, the two exercise forms always cancel each other
No, they generally coexist when workload is managed
Yes, unless every session is performed together
quiz.why: The updated review found no meaningful compromise in hypertrophy or maximal strength, though explosive strength may be more sensitive.

sources.label: World Health Organization (2020) — Guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour
Schumann M et al. (2022) — Concurrent aerobic and strength training meta-analysis

lessons.title: Tracking your progress
lessons.summary: A useful log turns fuzzy memories into comparable evidence. Track performance and a few slow-changing outcomes, then judge trends.

blocks.text: By the end, you can use a log to choose your next weight or rep target. Memory turns last month’s training into guesswork; tracking gives [[progressive overload]] a scoreboard.
Track the inputs you can act on

Record the exercise, load, completed reps, and your effort estimate. Add a short note when equipment, range, pain, or technique changed. Those details make later comparisons fair. A log is most useful when it records the task you actually performed, not the heroic version your brain edits overnight.

blocks.title: Don't Track Progress LIKE THIS!
blocks.why: Watch: avoiding misleading progress tracking (Renaissance Periodization).

left.title: Strong signals
items: More clean reps at the same load
The same reps with more load
Repeated progress across comparable sessions
Better control with the same task

right.title: Noisy signals
items: One unusually energetic workout
A different machine with different numbers
Extra reps from a shorter movement
A single scale reading after a salty meal

blocks.text: LiftLog does the boring part

items: Previous-set prefill shows the last weight and reps beside today’s set.
Workout history lets you compare several sessions instead of trusting one memory.
The body-weight chart shows a [[trend]] more clearly than isolated readings.
Progress photos and measurements can add context when appearance is a goal.

params.title: Look at the trend, not every wiggle
params.note: Made-up values show how short-term readings can bounce around a slower trend.

blocks.caption: Illustration: one measurement can move opposite to the longer pattern.

blocks.text: Body weight can change from food, fluid, and timing. Compare readings taken under similar conditions, and use the longer pattern. Photos also vary with lighting, pose, and distance. Standardising those details makes them more useful. None of these measures deserves daily emotional authority.

blocks.title: A simple post-workout review
blocks.text: After saving the workout, ask three questions: Did any lift improve? Did technique stay comparable? Did fatigue affect several exercises? Then leave the log alone until it is time to plan the next session.

Tracking should support decisions, not become homework with a barbell. Start with weights and reps because LiftLog already captures them. Add effort notes when they help. Add body weight, measurements, or photos only if they connect to your goal. Review patterns periodically, then make one change at a time.

takeaways: Log exercise, load, reps, and useful context so sessions remain comparable.
LiftLog’s previous-set prefill makes small performance targets visible.
Judge repeated trends, not one workout, weigh-in, photo, or measurement.
Track only information that can guide a decision tied to your goal.

quiz.q: Today’s machine uses different numbers from last week’s machine. What is the safest conclusion?
options: The larger number proves immediate progress
The sessions are not directly comparable
The smaller number proves muscle loss
quiz.why: Different machines can change the task and displayed load. Treat the comparison cautiously and keep future sessions consistent.

quiz.q: One body-weight reading jumps after an unusual meal. What should guide your decision?
options: The longer trend under similar conditions
That single reading by itself
A random change to the workout plan
quiz.why: Short-term readings can move for reasons unrelated to tissue change. Comparable measurements and the longer trend are more informative.

sources.label: American College of Sports Medicine (2009) — Progression models in resistance training
Helms ER et al. (2020) — Methods for regulating and monitoring resistance training

glossary.def: Gradually increasing a useful training challenge as your body adapts.
A method that builds repetitions within a range before increasing weight.
The amount of training work performed, often estimated with weekly hard sets.
A challenging working set performed close enough to your clean-rep limit to provide a useful stimulus.
How often you train a muscle or perform a type of session within a period.
The way a program distributes muscles or movement types across training days.
Reps in reserve: your estimate of how many clean repetitions remained when a set ended.
The point where you cannot complete another clean repetition in that set.
A repeated lack of progress across comparable sessions, rather than one poor performance.
A brief period of reduced training stress used to manage fatigue and support recovery.
Combining aerobic exercise and strength training within the same overall program.
A possible reduction in some adaptations when demanding aerobic and strength training compete for recovery.
The longer direction shown by several measurements, rather than one isolated reading.
